questions.question_text: Which of these is an equation?

options.why: Counted the $+$ sign as the link between two sides; only an equals sign makes an equation.
Treated two quantities joined by an operation as balanced, but there is still no equals sign.
Assumed any statement containing a pronumeral must be an equation.

questions.solution_text:
$9k = 45$ has an equals sign with an expression on each side.
The other three have no equals sign, so they are expressions.

questions.question_text:
Zara writes $9c + 4 =$ and calls it an equation.
Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is not an equation, because the RHS is missing.
It is an equation, because it contains an equals sign.
options.why: Uses the equals sign alone as the test, ignoring that both sides need an expression.

options.text: It is an equation, because $9c + 4$ is an expression.
options.why: Checks only the LHS and assumes one expression plus an equals sign is enough.

options.text: It is not an equation, because it contains a pronumeral.
options.why: Believes equations cannot contain pronumerals, confusing them with number facts.

questions.solution_text:
$9c + 4 =$
There is no expression to the right of the equals sign, so nothing is being equated.
It is not an equation.

options.text: Yes, because it has an equals sign with an expression on each side.
No, because an equation must contain a pronumeral.
options.why: Assumes a statement with no pronumeral cannot be an equation.

options.text: No, because it has already been worked out.
options.why: Thinks an equation must have something left to find.

options.text: Yes, because it contains a subtraction.
options.why: Uses the operation sign rather than the equals sign as the test.

questions.solution_text:
$20 - 4 = 16$
The LHS is the expression $20 - 4$ and the RHS is the expression $16$.
It is an equation.

questions.question_text: Which of these is an equation?

options.why: Mistakes an expression containing several terms for an equation, although it has no equals sign.
Checks for an equals sign but ignores the missing expression on the RHS.
Assumes a pronumeral alone makes an equation.

questions.solution_text:
$11 = 3p - 7$ has an equals sign with an expression on each side, so it is an equation.
The other statements either have no equals sign or have a missing RHS.

questions.question_text: Is $7h + 3 = 24$ an expression or an equation?

options.text: An equation, because an equals sign joins two expressions.
An expression, because it contains a pronumeral.
options.why: Uses the presence of a pronumeral to classify the statement and ignores the equals sign.

options.text: An expression, because $7h$ and $3$ are unlike terms.
options.why: Uses the types of terms on the LHS instead of checking whether an equals sign joins two expressions.

options.text: Neither, because the two sides do not look the same.
options.why: Assumes the expressions on both sides must look identical for a statement to be an equation.

questions.solution_text:
$7h + 3 = 24$
An equals sign joins an expression on each side, so it is an **equation**.

questions.question_text: For $5 + n = 13$, the solution is $n =$ what value?

options.why: Adds $5$ to $13$ instead of finding the number that adds to $5$ to make $13$.
Copies the RHS without allowing for the $5$ already added to $n$.
Subtracts $13$ from $5$ in the wrong order.

questions.solution_text:
The solution is $n = 8$ because $5 + 8 = 13$.
This value makes the two sides equal.

questions.question_text: Which statement about $y + 6 = 6 + y$ is correct?

options.text: It is an equation, and it is true for every value of $y$.
It is not an equation, because both sides are the same expression.
options.why: Assumes the two sides of an equation must look different from each other.

options.text: It is an expression, because there is nothing to find.
options.why: Uses "can I find one value?" as the test instead of looking for an equals sign.

options.text: It is an equation with the single solution $y = 0$.
options.why: Assumes every equation has exactly one solution and picks the simplest value.

questions.solution_text:
$y + 6 = 6 + y$
There is an equals sign with an expression on each side, so it is an equation.
Adding in either order gives the same total, so the sides are equal for every value of $y$.
